Integer powers:
A power a^n with a positive integer n means a multiplied by itself n times. For a ≠ 0, a^0 = 1 and a^(-n) = 1/a^n, so 2^(-3) = 1/8.

For the same base: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m / a^n = a^(m−n), and (a^m)^n = a^(m×n). For the same exponent: (ab)^n = a^n × b^n and (a/b)^n = a^n / b^n. A fraction with a negative exponent is flipped: (a/b)^(-n) = (b/a)^n.

A negative base with an odd exponent gives a negative result, and with an even exponent gives a positive result.
Scientific notation:
A number is in scientific notation when it is written as a × 10^n, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer. Large numbers have a positive n, for example 45 000 = 4.5 × 10^4. Numbers between 0 and 1 have a negative n, for example 0.00032 = 3.2 × 10^(-4).

To multiply, multiply the front numbers and add the exponents. To divide, divide the front numbers and subtract the exponents. If the front number leaves the range 1 to 10, adjust it: 30 × 10^7 = 3 × 10^8.

To add or subtract, first write both numbers with the same power of 10.
Square roots:
The square root of a ≥ 0, written √a, is the non-negative number whose square is a. For example, √49 = 7. The equation x^2 = a with a > 0 has two solutions, x = √a and x = −√a. For any real x, √(x^2) = |x|.

Product rule: √(ab) = √a × √b. Quotient rule: √(a/b) = √a / √b for b > 0. To simplify, take out the largest perfect square factor: √72 = 6√2. Roots with the same radical part can be added: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2.

Note that √(a + b) is not equal to √a + √b.
Roots of higher order:
The n-th root of a is the number which, multiplied by itself n times, gives a. For example, ∛27 = 3 and ∜16 = 2. An odd root exists for every real number: ∛(−8) = −2. An even root exists only for numbers that are zero or positive.

The product and quotient rules also work for higher roots: ∛(ab) = ∛a × ∛b. To simplify, take out the largest perfect n-th power factor: ∛54 = 3∛2.

Roots can be written as fractional exponents: the n-th root of a is a^(1/n), and a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))^m. For example, 16^(3/4) = 8.
